name: Battersea Grammar School
text: Your train passes near the site of Battersea Grammar School, on the train's {side}. Founded in Battersea in 1875, the school moved to larger premises in Streatham in 1936, and closed in 1977 when it merged with Rosa Bassett School, a girls' grammar school, to form Furzedown Secondary School in Tooting.

name: Mitcham Cricket Green
text: Your train passes near Mitcham Cricket Green, on the train's {side}, where cricket has been played since 1685. Touring Australian teams of the 19th century stayed at the Cricketers pub, which overlooked the green, and practised on the green, and its pavilion, built in 1904, is one of the few cut off from their ground by a road.

name: BedZED
text: Your train passes near BedZED, the Beddington Zero Energy Development, on the train's {side}. Designed by the architect Bill Dunster and built from 2000 to 2002, its 82 homes made up the first large community designed to give off no carbon emissions, and it was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2003.

name: Wilderness Island
text: Your train passes near Wilderness Island, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of almost three hectares on the island between the rivers Wandle and Wrythe in Carshalton. A fish pond survives from a public garden that was once here, and kingfishers and the rare hornet clearwing moth can be found.

name: Oakleigh Way
text: Your train passes Oakleigh Way, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of less than a hectare in Mitcham. It was once a railway depot and sidings, and is now birch woodland with scrub and grassland, where weld and zigzag clover grow.

name: St Leonard's Church, Streatham
text: Your train passes near St Leonard's Church, Streatham, on the train's {side}, the parish church of a parish named in the Domesday Book. The lower part of its tower dates from the 14th century; almost all the rest was rebuilt in 1830 and 1831, and the church was restored after a fire gutted it on May 5th 1975.

name: Du Cane Court
text: Your train passes near Du Cane Court, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco block of 677 flats on Balham High Road. When it was built in 1937 it was thought to be the largest privately owned block of flats in Europe, and many music hall stars of the 1930s and 1940s lived there, among them the comedian Tommy Trinder.

name: St Luke's Church, West Norwood
text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church, West Norwood, on the train's {side}, one of four "Waterloo churches" named after the four Gospel writers. Designed by Francis Octavius Bedford as a result of the Church Building Act of 1818, it was consecrated on July 25th 1825, on a triangular site where Norwood Road forks.

name: South London Botanical Institute
text: Your train passes near the South London Botanical Institute, on the train's {side}, founded in 1910 by Allan Octavian Hume in a large Victorian house on Norwood Road. It has changed little since, keeping its library, a herbarium of pressed plants and a small botanic garden with more than 500 species.

name: Half Moon, Herne Hill
text: Your train passes the Half Moon, on the train's {side}, a corner pub of 1896 that is one of only 270 pubs on CAMRA's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors. The poet Dylan Thomas drank there, and for nearly 50 years it was a live music venue: U2 played there three times in 1980.

name: Dulwich College
text: Your train passes near Dulwich College, on the train's {side}, founded on June 21st 1619 by the Elizabethan actor Edward Alleyn as the College of God's Gift, to educate 12 poor scholars. It grew into a large school from 1857, and moved into its present buildings in 1870.

name: Six Pillars
text: Your train passes near Six Pillars, on the train's {side}, a modernist house built from 1932 to 1934 for John Leakey, headmaster of Dulwich College Preparatory School. Its architect, Valentine Harding of the Tecton group, based it on Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye, but used London stock brick so it wouldn't stand out among its Victorian neighbours.

name: Royal Watermen's Almshouses
text: Your train passes near the Royal Watermen's Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built in 1840 and 1841 by the Company of Watermen and Lightermen of the City of London for retired freemen and their widows. They are the oldest Victorian almshouses in Penge; the residents moved to Hastings in 1973, and the buildings became private homes.

name: St George's Church, Beckenham
text: Your train passes near St George's Church, Beckenham, on the train's {side}. First built in the 12th century, it was rebuilt from 1885 to 1887 by the local architect W. Gibbs Bartleet, and its pinnacled tower, finished in 1903, is the focal point of Beckenham High Street.

name: Beckenham Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Beckenham Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1876 as the Crystal Palace District Cemetery. The cricketer W. G. Grace and the businessman Thomas Crapper are buried there.

name: National Sports Centre, Crystal Palace
text: Your train passes near the National Sports Centre, on the train's {side}, opened in Crystal Palace Park in 1964. It stands on the site of the ground where FA Cup finals were played from 1895 to 1914, and its athletics stadium has also staged concerts by Bruce Springsteen and the Sex Pistols.

name: Crystal Palace transmitting station
text: Your train passes near the Crystal Palace transmitting station, on the train's {side}, the main television transmitter for London, on the site of a television station run by John Logie Baird from 1933. Standing on a hill 109 metres high, it is the highest structure above sea level in London.

name: West Norwood Cemetery
text: Your train passes near West Norwood Cemetery, on the train's {side}, consecrated on December 7th 1837 and one of London's "Magnificent Seven" Victorian cemeteries. Its 69 listed monuments and buildings include a Greek Orthodox burial ground with 19 listed mausoleums and monuments.

name: St John the Evangelist, Upper Norwood
text: Your train passes near the Church of St John the Evangelist, Upper Norwood, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Gothic Revival church built from 1878 to 1887 to the designs of John Loughborough Pearson. It replaced a large iron church moved to the site in 1875 to serve the new suburb.

name: Holy Innocents Church, South Norwood
text: Your train passes near Holy Innocents Church, South Norwood, on the train's {side}, built in 1894 and 1895 to the designs of George Frederick Bodley, in imitation of the late Gothic Perpendicular style. The tower he planned for it was never built.

name: No. 1 Croydon
text: Your train passes near the "50p Building", on the train's {side}, the 24-storey tower next to East Croydon station that was first called the NLA Tower and is also known as the "Threepenny Bit". Designed by Richard Seifert and Partners and finished in 1970, it gets its distinctive look from floors with cut-off corners, set one above another at alternating angles.

name: Fairfield Halls
text: Your train passes near Fairfield Halls, on the train's {side}, an arts centre opened in 1962 with a large concert hall often used for BBC recordings. It stands on Croydon's old "Fair Field", home to a well-known fair until about 1860, above disused railway cuttings that once led from the line to Brighton to Croydon Central station.

name: Whitgift School
text: Your train passes near Whitgift School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1596 by John Whitgift, Archbishop of Canterbury, and opened in 1600. It moved here in 1931 to Haling Park, once the home of Lord Howard of Effingham, who commanded the English fleet against the Spanish Armada.

name: Purley War Memorial Hospital
text: Your train passes near Purley War Memorial Hospital, on the train's {side}. It began as a cottage hospital with eight beds, opened by Princess Helena, and after the First World War it reopened in 1922 as the district's war memorial hospital, with 22 beds.

name: Purley Council Offices
text: Your train passes near the former Purley Council Offices, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Neo-Georgian building that cost £30,000. The Lord Mayor of London opened it on November 8th 1930 as the headquarters of the Coulsdon and Purley Urban District Council.

name: Coulsdon North station
text: Your train passes the site of Coulsdon North station, on the train's {side}. It opened on November 5th 1899 as "Stoats Nest and Cane Hill", changed its name three times, and closed on October 3rd 1983 when the line to Brighton was resignalled.

name: Coulsdon Town station
text: Coulsdon Town station opened as Smitham on January 1st 1904 and kept that name until May 22nd 2011. It sits on a sharp curve, where the line to Tattenham Corner swings away westwards from the main line to Brighton.

name: Croydon, Merstham and Godstone Railway embankment
text: Your train passes near an embankment of the Croydon, Merstham and Godstone Railway, on the train's {side}. Opened in 1805 as an extension of the horse-drawn Surrey Iron Railway, the line ran to quarries near Merstham until 1838; this embankment at Coulsdon is eight metres high.

name: Foxley Wood
text: Your train passes near Foxley Wood, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of more than 11 hectares, partly ancient woodland of oak and ash, with patches of chalk grassland. The local council bought it in the 1930s to keep it as Green Belt, and badgers and roe deer live there.

name: Whyteleafe
text: Your train passes near Whyteleafe, on the train's {side}, a village in a dry valley of the North Downs with three railway stations on two lines. It takes its name from the whitebeam trees that grow here, whose leaves are white underneath.

name: Elmhurst School
text: Your train passes near Elmhurst School, on the train's {side}, a preparatory school that grew from two schools founded in 1869. One of them, run by the sisters Clarissa and Florence Prince, counted the young P. G. Wodehouse among its pupils in the 1880s, and moved into the house called Elmhurst in 1894.

name: Riddlesdown
text: Your train passes near Riddlesdown, on the train's {side}, a place recorded as Ridelesdowne in 1331; the "Riddle" part is thought to come from Middle English for "cleared woodland". Most of its houses were built in the 1930s by John Laing, some with an Art Deco touch, and Fred Perry opened its tennis club in June 1938.

name: Riddlesdown Common
text: Your train runs beside Riddlesdown Common, on the train's {side}, 43 hectares near the northern end of the North Downs, owned by the City of London Corporation, most of it a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Neolithic stone axes have been found there, and a trig point on top shows it is 525 feet above sea level.

name: Anerley Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Anerley Town Hall, on the train's {side}, an Italianate building by George Elkington, opened on April 30th 1879 as the vestry hall of St Paul's, Anerley. It became the headquarters of Penge Urban District in 1900; its assembly hall has an unusual hammerbeam roof tied with wrought-iron rods.

name: Croydon Canal, Betts Park
text: Your train is following the course of the Croydon Canal, which crossed Penge Common along what is now this line through Penge West; a stretch of it survives in Betts Park, on the train's {side}. After the canal closed, the London and Croydon Railway, at first an atmospheric railway, was built largely along its course and opened in 1839.

name: St Christopher's Hospice
text: Your train passes near St Christopher's Hospice, on the train's {side}, founded in 1967 by Cicely Saunders, whose work is the basis of the modern hospice movement. Its early staff began the first hospice home care, and one of them, Florence Wald, took the idea to the United States.

name: Crystal Palace Dinosaurs
text: Your train passes the Crystal Palace Dinosaurs, on the train's {side}, unveiled in 1854 as the first dinosaur sculptures in the world. Designed by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins with Sir Richard Owen, they show 15 kinds of extinct animal, only three of them true dinosaurs, and are listed Grade I.

name: Mayow Park
text: Your train passes near Mayow Park, on the train's {side}, opened in 1878 as Sydenham Recreation Ground on land owned by the Mayow family. It is the oldest park in the borough of Lewisham, and the tea merchant Frederick Horniman was on the committee formed to find the money and the land for it.

name: Horniman Museum
text: Your train passes near the Horniman Museum, on the train's {side}, opened in 1901 by the tea trader Frederick Horniman for his collection of some 30,000 objects. Designed by Charles Harrison Townsend, it is known for its natural history displays and musical instruments, and it was Museum of the Year in 2022.

name: Rivoli Ballroom
text: Your train passes near the Rivoli Ballroom, on the train's {side}, opened in July 1913 as the Crofton Park Picture Palace. After its last film in 1957 it became a dance hall, reopening on Boxing Day 1959 with a sprung floor of Canadian maple, and it keeps its red velvet, flock wallpaper and chandeliers.
